supervision, nor has it the ability to take care of such a large number of 
monuments. I have seen every monumen t in India. The Raza Library at 
Rampur I can talk of. Will the Minister review this seriously and try to have a 
new worthwhile and extensive policy, including the role of private industry

*262. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE:  Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have introduced any Night Shelter Scheme for 
the shelterless and pavement dwellers; 
(b) if so, when the scheme was introduced; and 
.   (c) the funds released so far, by Government for this scheme State and 
year-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Night Shelter Scheme was introduced in 1988-89 to provide Night 
Shelter and Pay & Use toilet facilities to urban shelterless. 
The Scheme was modified in August 1992 to cover all urban centres 
having concentration of footpath dwe llers/homeless and renamed as "Shelter 
& Sanitation Facilities for footpath Dwellers in Urban Areas." Since October, 
2002, the scheme has been revised and renamed as "Night Shelter for Urban 
Shelterless." The scheme is now limited to construction of composite Night 
Shelters with community toilets and baths for urban shelterless. This is a 
demand driven scheme and its implementation is undertaken by the State 
Government or local municipal bodies  or State sponsored agencies and 
proposals are mooted by them. Under the scheme, Government of India 
subsidy of 50% of the cost of construction (subject to cost ceiling of Rs. 
20,000 per bed) is given to implementing agencies

Tribals residing in forests 
†*269. SHRI ISAM SINGH: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that tribal people residing in forests remain naked 
even today; 
(b) if so, the number thereof; and 
(c) the details of Government's action plan to improve their standard of 
living? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH) (a) to 
(c) There are two Scheduled Tribes in  Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the 
Jarawas and Sentinelese who are residing  in forests and remain almost naked 
even today. The Jarawas and Sentineles e are declared as aboriginal tribes 
since 1956. They were along with other tribes declared Scheduled Tribes in 
1959. As per 2001 Census, the Jarawas are 240 and the Sentinelese are 39 in 
number estimated. The Sentinelese are still hostile and live in isolation in 
North Sentinel Island. The Andaman and Nicobar Administration provide gift 
etc. from a distance. Jarawas are living in South and Middle Andaman. 
Andaman and Nicobar Administration has informed that the population of 
Jarawas is now 266. Andaman and Nicobar Islands declared certain territories 
as reserve for aboriginal people of the Island and some parts of South and 
Middle Andaman were reserv ed for Jarawas. The Jarawas were hostile but 
have come in contact with outsiders si nce 1997. The contact of Jarawas with 
outsiders led to some problems such as measles, skin diseases etc. 
The Andaman and Nicobar Administration has taken action for the welfare 
of the Jarawas:— 
1. Exclusive natural resources base i.e. Jarawa tribal forest reserve has 
been increased from 847 sq. kms. to 1028 sq. kms. for their foraging. 
2. Exclusive marine resource base has also been increased by declaring 
coastal water up to 5 km. from high tide mark as tribal reserve. 
3. Jarawa tribal reseve has been carved out taking into account natural 
features like hill range peaks, creeks etc. as far as practicable so that 
boundaries of the reserve area is intelligible to all concerned

thereby trespass into reserve area is avoided. There will be no .        
intervention in the day to day life of the Jarawas. 
4. Andaman Trunk Road belt has been decreased from 200 meters on 
either side of the tar road to only 30 meters from the center line of 
the road on either side. 
5. Enforcement measures have been  intensified by the Police and 
Forest to protect the Jarawa resource base in the Forest and coastal 
water. 
6. Police, trained anthropologists and other welfare functionaries are 
pressed into service for regular patrolling at vulnerable places to 
prevent unauthorized contact of non-tribals with the Jarawas. 
7. Sites of Police, Forest and PWD are reviewed and rationalized by 
relocating some of them as far away  as possible from the vicinity of 
Jarawas territory to avoid non-Jarawa's proximity to Jarawas. 
8. Standing Health Team consisting of experience and selected doctors 
has been constituted which visits the Jarawas in the forest 
periodically to make assessment of their health and provide required 
care in the Jarawa area itself to the extent feasible. 
9. Trained health workers are deployed in the field daily to provide 
treatment for minor ailments in situ and thereby avoiding evacuation 
of Jarawas to the hospital for minor ailment. 
 
10. Jarawa patients are shifted to hospital only when it is inevitable 
keeping in view their health interest/to save their life. 
11. Separate/exclusive hospital wards for Jarawas have been provided 
and such wards are declared as Trib al Reserve, the entry into which 
by non-tribals is prohibited without the permit from the competent 
authority.

*275. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state:

judicial accountability as per the resolution passed by the Apex Court;

(c) if so, whether any steps are being considered to stop the erosion of 
people's trust; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H,R. BHARDWAJ) (a) 
to (d) Attention of the Government has been drawn, from time to time, to the 
question of enforcing judicial accountability. 
2. The issue was discussed at the Conference of Chief Justices held in 
1990 and on the basis of the broad consensus emerging out of the 
deliberations, the Chief Justice of India summed up the position as follows: 
"The Chief Justice of the High Co urt has the competence to receive 
complaints against the conduct of the Judges of his court and when he 
receives any, he would look into it for fi nding out if it deserves to be closely 
looked into. Where he is satisfied that the matter requires to be examined, he 
shall have facts ascertained in such  manner as he considers appropriate 
keeping the nature of allegations in view and if he is of the opinion that the 
matter is such that it should be reported to the Chief Justice of India, he shall 
do so. 
The Chief Justice of India shall act in a similar manner in regard to 
complaints relating to conduct of Judges of the Supreme Court and in regard 
to conduct of Chief Justices of the High Courts. On the basis of the facts 
ascertained, the Chief Justice of the High  Court or the Supr eme Court, as the 
case may be, shall take such appropriat e action as may be considered proper, 
keeping the interests of the judiciary as the paramount consideration." 
3. The complaints received against the Judges of the Supreme Court 
and the High Courts are dealt with in the manner indicated above. The 
Judges Inquiry Act, 1968 specifies the procedure to deal with misconduct/

misdemeanour of Judges of the Supreme Court/High Courts, but Government 
has no constitutional competence to order enquiry against them.

Report on ICHR 
*278. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have received an interim report of the one-man 
Review Committee of the Indian Council for Historical Research (ICHR); 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH) (a) to (c) The one-man  Review Committee enquiring into 
the affairs of the Indian Council of Hi storical Research (ICHR) has so far 
submitted two interim reports. These relate to the "non-publication/stoppage 
of volumes of Towards Freedom' Project by ICHR"; and, on the "non-
submission of research work by scholars, who were given Fellowships by the 
ICHR during the period between 1995-96 and 2000-01, as highlighted in the 
report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India for 2002-03". 
42 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In its interim report on the 'Towards Freedom' Project, the Committee has 
observed that attempts were made to scuttle the project through stoppage of 
funds and interruption in the publication of the volumes. The Committee has 
recommended the completion of the project within 24 months and the 
constitution of an Editorial Board with an eminent historian as the General 
Editor. The Committee has also recommended the streamlining of the 
procedures of publication and has suggested that the Government take a view 
regarding the present Council, including its Chairman. 
On the issue of the 'non-submission of research work by scholars', the 
Committee has observed irregularities in the award of the Senior Research 
Fellowships and the National Fellowships, such as no proper representation 
to the different regions of the count ry, SCs/STs, women and the minorities. 
The Committee has recommended a St anding Search Committee to award 
National Fellowships, and the institution of a system of nominations to the 
Senior Search Fellowships as well as the computerisation of the fellowships 
programme and, the travel grant programme. The Committee has also 
recommended the recovery of fellowship grants from the defaulters. 
The Government has accepted the re commendations of the Committee in 
the interim report on the "non-publication/stoppage of volumes of Towards 
Freedom Project", and the ICHR has been directed to take action on the 
same. The interim report of the Committee on "non-submission of research 
work by scholars" is under examination.

*279. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether UNESCO has made concrete suggestions for upkeep of Taj 
Mahal at Agra and maintenance of its surroundings and environment;

THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY) (a) Yes Sir. 
Based on the UNESCO-ICOMOS Joint Monitoring Mission, the UNESCO 
World Heritage Committee in its meeting held in June-July 2004 has made 
the following recommendations concerning the World Heritage properties 
Taj Mahal, Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri. 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2005] 
(i)  Set up a body to coordinate and address all the conservation and 
development challenges of the three World Heritage properties in 
the Agra District by involving all the stakeholders. 
(ii) Evaluate and redefine the World Heritage protective boundaries and 
management guidelines pertaining to the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort. 
(iii)  Integrate the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort as one protected World 
Heritage area to ensure better ma nagement of the property, with a 
possible inclusion of Fatehpur Sikri subject to a broader regional 
planning scheme. 
(iv)   Elaborate a comprehensive site management plan, including a 
specific visitor management plan, based on a regional plan for 
conservation and development of the World Heritage properties, and 
ensure its implementation. 
(v) Improve the on-site interpretation and visitor management at the 
World Heritage properties. 
(vi) Set up on-site monitoring mechanisms, to assess the impact of urban 
development on the World Heritage values of the properties and 
their surrounding areas so as to integrate the protection of urban 
landscape into the overall heritage protection mechanism. 
(vii) Organise a National Workshop on the elaboration of Site 
Management Plans for the preparation of the World Heritage 
extension(s), including the upgrading of the protective boundary and 
buffer zones. 
(c) Steps are being taken for preparation of comprehensive site 
management plan for all the three World Heritage Sites.

Saffronisation of school syllabus 
2038. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of controversy regarding saffronisation of school syllabus 
during the last regime; 
(b) whether it has affected the curriculum in any manners; and 
(c) if so, in what manner Government would rectify the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI): (a) to (c) The 
National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCFSE) was brought 
out by the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
in the year 2000. The textbooks developed by NCERT under the NCFSE-
2000 engaged public and academic attention on account of several 
inadequacies. A panel of three eminent historians was constituted by the 
Government to conduct a review of NCERT history textbooks because of 
reported biases and inadequacies th erein. The Executiv e Committee of the 
NCERT in July, 2004 considered the Report of the panel. In view of the 
advanced stage of the current academ ic session, it was decided that the 
existing NCERT history textbooks, excluding the controversial portions, 
would be used by the students of the CBSE affiliated schools alongwith the 
advisory prepared by NCERT. Five copies each of the history textbooks used 
in the CBSE schools prior to the introduction of the controversial history 
textbooks were also distributed free of cost to all the schools for teachers for 
use as reference books. 
To comply with the decision of th e Executive Body for restoring the 
NCERT textbooks after effecting approp riate modifications in line with the 
existing curriculum for the academic  session 2005-06, the following 
Committees were constituted by the NCERT:— 
74 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) A History Committee was constituted for making necessary 
recommendations to review pre-2000 NCERT histroy textbooks. The old 
NCERT history textbooks, after incorporation of necessary changes based on 
the recommendations of this Committee, would be restored during 2005-06. 
(b) In respect of textbooks other than history textbooks, Quick Review 
Committees were also constituted by NCERT and errors pointed out by these 
Committees have been incorporated as errata in the NCERT textbooks for the 
next academic year. 
In keeping with the 5-yearly mandate of the National Policy on Education 
(NPE) as well as the decision of the Executive Committee of NCERT, a 
review of the NCFSE has been initiated by the NCERT in the current 
academic year. For this purpose, a National Steering Group of eminent 
scholars, activists and teachers has been constituted by the NCERT. In 
addition, 21 National Focus Groups covering different subject areas, issues of 
structural reorganization of the education, those of national concern such as 
gender, problems of the SC/ST children, etc. have also been constituted. 
The Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) has separately set up a 
committee on 10.9.2004, inter alia, to suggest an appr opriate regulatory 
mechanism for institutionalizing the issu e of preparation of textbooks and 
curricular material. 
The recommendations of the National Steering Group/Focus Groups and 
those of the Committee set up by CABE would be important inputs in a 
revised NCFSE.

2046. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that more than 10 per cent girls in the country get 
married before attaining the age of 14, according to studies conducted by 
Population Council of India; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to impose ban on such underage 
marriages by educating the parents through Government agencies/NGOs?

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH) (a) Yes, Sir. 
As per the report of International Institute for Population Sciences, the 
percentage of currently married women in the age group of 25-29 got married 
by the age of 13 years is 12.1 and th at the percentage of women in the age 
group of 20-24 has been dropped to 8.9 and in the age group of 15-19 to 4.7. 
(b) The Government is taking all necessary steps to reduce the child 
marriages. 
83

from the country. Such as, 
* State Governments have been asked for strict implementation of Child 
Marriage (Restraint) Act, 1929; 
* State Governments have been asked to take necessary measures to 
prevdnt child marriages in their States; 
* The proposal for amendment to the Child Marriage (Restraint) Act, 
1929 is presently under consideration of a Parliamentary Standing 
Committee which would help in better implementation of the Act;

* A strong media campaign is being launched by the Department of 
Women and Child Development especi ally to target prevention of 
child marriages in the forthcoming festival season of Akshaya Teej;

Examination stress 
2050. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR : Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the examination stress continues to take a heavy toll of life of 
students, year after year, despite implementation of the recommendations of 
the Examination Reforms Commission; 
(b) if so, the number of suicides committed by students in Delhi and other 
States so far during the examinations this year and the comparative figures 
for the last three years; and 
(c) the steps taken/being taken to ease such stress further? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M.A.A. FATMI) (a) Yes, Sir. 
However, it is not only examination stress but various other contributory 
factors such as parental pressure increasing competition and fast changing 
social and economic conditions wh ich at times compel students to 
depression. 
(b) There are three suicide reports pub lished in the newspapers wherein 
examination stress has been stated to be the cause of suicide by the students. 
(c) The steps taken to reduce stress among students are as follows: 
(i) Launching of 'helpline' one month before the commencement of 
examination also before the declaration of results. 
(ii) Publication of sample question papers and marking schemes to 
familiarize students and teachers about the nature of questions and 
question papers 
(iii) Elimination of ov erall aggregation of marks to reduce unhealthy 
competition among students. 
(iv) Introduction of comprehensive and continuous school based 
evaluation. 
(v) Providing facility of compartment examination in two subjects in 
class X and one subject in class XII. 
(vi) Providing three chances of co mpartment examination for class X 
and XII.

to provide more internal choices of questions.

group of women in difficult circumstances through a home-based holistic and 
integrated approach.

Pirated CDs and DVDs 
2093. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that pirated CDs and DVDs are easily accessible in 
the open market which are ruining the music and film industry; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to check this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI 
S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) and (b) According to Federation of lndian Chamber 
of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) the revenue loss from film piracy is about 
Rs. 1200 crores annually. As far as Musi c Industry is concerned, the Indian 
Music Industry (IMI) has informed that  the size of the music industry has 
fallen from Rs. 1000 crores in 1999 to Rs.500 crores in 2004 due to piracy. 
The Ministry does not have any data. 
(c)The Copyright Act, 1957, which falis under the purview of the Ministry 
of Human Resource Development contains, inter alia the legal provisions 
regarding copyright in cinematograph films and music. The responsibility for 
dealing with offences under the Copyright Act rests with the police 
authorities of the State Governments and Union Territory Administrations. 
Copyright Enforcement cells have been set up in most States/UT 
Administrations headed by a senior police officer to deal with such offences. 
Apart from this, the Ministry of Information and Broadcastiang has taken 
the following steps to fight piracy in the film sector; 
• This Ministry has a Plan Scheme  to undertake activities relating to 
anti piracy measures. The Ministry has initiated action to formulate 
appropriate training modules for po lice officers to train them for 
anti-piracy. 
• In September 2001, Ministry of l&B brought together 
representatives of the film produ cers, multi-service operators and 
cable operators who have jointly resolved not to exhibit films 
without valid permission from the copyright holders. 
• Recognizing that high levels of entertainment tax lead to piracy, the 
Committee for Development of th e Entertainment Sector, a sub 
committee of the State Information Ministers' Conference, 
122 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA  SABHA 
recommended that the rate of entertainment tax be lowered to a 
ceiling of 45%. A number of States have suitably lowered their 
entertainment tax levels. 
• The Committee also recommended appointment of senior police 
officers in States to work in co -ordination with the entertainment 
industry, as nodal officers. 
• During the Budget of 2003-04, audio CDs were exempted from 
excise duty to do away with the pr ice advantage available to pirated 
CDs. 
• The Public Service Broadcasting Trust has been entrusted with the 
task of making a film on piracy. 
• The Cable Television Networks Regulation Act has been amended 
in 2000, to prohibit a Cable operator from transmitting or re-
transmitting any programme or channel for which the Copyright 
holder has not granted him a license. 
• This Ministry has requested Chief Secretaries of all States to advise 
District Magistrates and Superintendents of Police to include anti 
piracy measures in their monthly activity reports.

DASARI NARAYANA RAO); (a) No, Sir. Section 1-8 of the Mines and 
Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) enjoins

which the applicant proposes to make in the mines and in the industry based 
on the minerals while deciding merits of various applicants.

Problems of Jhuggis 
†2152. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any scheme to tackle the 
problem of increasing Jhuggies in the cities; and 
(b) the population inhabited in Jhuggies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
Slum development is a State subject . The State Governments formulate 
specific plans, programmes and schemes for development of slums in various 
towns/cities as per their priorities and ma ke necessary provisions therefor in 
their respective State Plans. However, with a view to ameliorate the living 
conditions of the slum dwellers, a programme known as National Slum 
Development Programme (NSDP) was launched at the national level by the 
Government in August, 1996 for the development of urban slums. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2005] 
Besides, a Centrally sponsored Scheme called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas 
Yojana (VAMBAY) was launched on 2.12.2001 with a view to ameliorating 
the conditions of the urban slum dwellers living below the poverty line who 
do not possess adequate shelter. The Scheme has the primary objective to 
facilitate the construction and upgradation of the dwelling units for the slum 
dwellers and to provide health and enabling urban environment through 
community toilets under Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, a component of the 
Scheme. 
(b) Slum Development being a State subject, State Governments survey 
and take stock of slums/jhuggies in their respective States. However, the 
Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO) conducted a one time 
study on slums in 1995-96 and brought out a report titled "a Compendium on 
India Slums-1996". According to this report the slum population of India is 
estimated to be 6.18 crores in 2001. 
An attempt was made for the first time during the Census of India, 2001 by 
the Registrar General of India to collect detailed data about slum population 
of the country but only in the cities/towns having 50.000 population or more 
based on 1991 census. As per the provisional figures of Census of India 2001, 
the slum population of such 607 towns/ cities of the country is 4.03 crores 
approximately.

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, it is shocking to know that 
close to one in every three babies, that die before they are four week's old in 
the world, die in India. Of the 26 milli on children born in India each year, 1.2 
million die in the first four weeks and 30  per cent of the world's 3.9 million 
neonatal deaths take place in India. Th is has been revealed recently by the 
State of India's Newborns Report. The current Neonatal Mortality Rate is

lakh maternal deaths globally, each ye ar, are in India. So, I urge upon the 
Government of India to immediately ta ke measures to reduce the Neonatal 
Mortality Rate in India by taking necessary measures.

Demand for implementation of integrated drinking water scheme 
at Hogenakal, Tamil Nadu 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Sir, Dharmapuri and Krishnagiri are the 
most backward districts in Tamil Nadu. There is no adequate drinking water 
facility. The ground water level has gone down considerably. Even the little 
water available is not potable. A high content of fluoride is present which will 
endanger the lives of human beings and cattle. 
Due to concerted efforts of our Chief Minister, the rain water harvesting 
has been undertaken. But there is no respite from drinking water shortage. 
There is a waterfall in Hogenakal in Dharmapuri district. It is an important 
204 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
tourist centre. The water falling in the falls can be exploited for drinking water. 
The integrated drinking water scheme at Hogenakal, which would entail 
considerable expenditure, will solve the drinking water problem of Dharmapuri 
and Krishnagiri districts. Since the State was reeling under drought and recent 
tsunami disaster, the State is not in a position to invest the money. But the 
State is taking all steps to implement the project. 
Only with the assistance of Central Government, the project can be 
implemented. Although the matter was raised in Parliament several times by 
me, yet no action has been taken by the Central Government. 
There are no major industries in the Dharmapuri and Krishnagiri districts 
and, as such, there are no employment op portunities. Agriculture is the main 
occupation there. Since there is no water, agricultural operations have been 
affected. People may be forced to migrate to other places. 
It is estimated that about Rs. 1300 crore will be involved in the 
implementation of this project. I urge upon the Central Government to fully 
assist the State Government in this regard or obtain the World Bank loan at 
the earliest. Thank you, Sir.

That this House approves the Procla mation issued by the President on the

Before I explain the circumstances in which the Government has had to 
bring this Resolution to this august House, may I state that the Constitution 
framers had recognized that the provisi ons of article 356, among others, were 
necessary to meet the exceptional si tuation where the break down of the 
constitutional machinery occurs in a State. 
Now, may I take this opportunity to narrate briefly the circumstances 
prevailing in Bihar which led to the imposition of President's rule in the State. 
Elections to the Legislative Assembly of Bihar were held on 3rd, 15th and 
23rd of February, 2005. The number of s eats won by different political parties 
in the State, as emerged after c ounting on 27th February, 2005 are as 
follows:—

Smt. Rabri Devi tendered her resignation as Chief Minister on 28th 
February, 2005. She was asked to contin ue by the Governor till alternative 
arrangements were made. The Governor of Bi har kept a watch on the 
political situation. He assessed the claims made for formation of a popular 
206 

[21 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Government by two major coalitions and finally sent a report to the President 
on 6th March, 2005. As per the Govern or's report, the RJD and its alliance 
had the support of 92 MLAs, whereas the NDA alliance also had the support 
of 92 MLAs. 
A delegation of the members of UP met the Governor on 28th February, 
2005 and submitted a letter stating t ha they would neither support the RJD 
nor the BJP in the formation of the Go vernment in Bihar. In a subsequent 
meeting with the Governor, they reiterat ed their stand. The Governor, in his 
report already tabled in this august House, along with the President's 
Proclamation, gave a detailed account of his meetings with representatives of 
various political parties/alliances and some independent MLAs, and an 
analysis of how no combination of political parties or a coalition was able to 
form a Government, which would have the confidence of the majority of the 
members in the newly-constituted Assembly. 
Briefly, due to claims and counter-claims of various parties and alliances, 
without any supporting evidence, the Governor in his report stated that he had 
explored all the possibilities and he was fu lly satisfied that no political party or 
coalition of parties or groups was able to substantiate a claim of majority in 
the Legislative Assembly. According to the Governor, it was a case of 
complete inability of any political party to form a stable Government 
commanding the confidence of the majori ty of the Members. Therefore, the 
Governor recommended that the newly constituted Assembly be kept in 
suspended animation for the present and requested the President of India to 
take appropriate action, as required. 
The Budget of the State of Bihar for the year 2005-06 was yet to be 
passed. It would not have been appropriate for the caretaker Government to 
take any action regarding the passing of the Budget or a Vote-on-Account. 
There would have been serious financial and constitutional crises if the 
Budget or the Vote-on-Account were not passed before 31st March, 2005. 
The Union Cabinet, therefore, in its meeting held on 7th March, 2005 
considered the report of the Governor and the situation prevailing in Bihar, 
and decided to recommend to the President to issue a Proclamation under 
article 356 of the Constitution for imposing the President's rule in the State 
and keeping the State Legislative Assembly under suspended animation. 
On 7th March, 2005, the President was pleased to issue a Proclamation

under article 356(1) of the Constituti on imposing the President's rule in 
relation to the State of Bihar and keep ing the State Legislative Assembly 
under suspended animation. 
With these words, I commend, Sir, that the Proclamation issued on 7th 
March, 2005 under article 356 of the C onstitution in relation to the State of 
Bihar be approved by this august House. A copy of the Proclamation, as 
stipulated under the Constitution, along with consequential Order, is placed on 
the Table of the House. In keeping wi th the conventions, a copy of the 
Governor's report recommending issuance of the Proclamation is also placed 
on the Table of the House.
